A BOOKKEEPER DECAMPS. Special District to The Chicago Tribune. LA FAVETTE, Ind., Aug. 8.—To-day at noon Thomas Jamison, temporarily bookkeeper for Hamlin & Co., confectioners, left the store to deposit $900 firm money. He did not deposit it, and has not since turned up. He left $100 with a friend to give Mrs. Jamison, with a message not to be unasy until she heard from him. It is thought he went to Indianapolis. Jamison has always born a good character, and friends are at a loss to account for his disappearance and conduct. STEAMER FIRED ON. CINCINNATI, O., Aug. 8.—Fourteen shots were fired into the steamer Handy yesterday morning when she was approaching Portsmouth, O. The shots came from a wagon on the road close to the river bank. The pilot was compelled to lie flat. The balls entered the cabin, and one barely missed a lady passenger. The shots also entered the engine-room. No cause can be assigned for the attack. Efforts have been made to arrest the criminals. LAWLESS NEGROES.
LAWLESS NEGROES.
CINCINNATI, O., Aug. 8.—Two negroes have been causing a reign of terror in the vicinity of Oakley and Madisonville, near the city, within the past two or three nights. They have assaulted and robbed half a dozen people, two or three of whom they have shot and wounded. Citizens have gathered, and to-day it was reported that they had the negroes surrounded in the woods and expected to capture them.

SAFE-BLOWERS ARRESTED.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
LA SALLE, Ill., Aug. 8.—John McGowen and Thomas Garrity, arrested in this city Friday night last for blowing open the safe of Thomas Drew, of Lostau, and taking therefrom $3,000, were examined this afternoon and put under $2,000 bonds to appear before the Grand Jury. The evidence is very strong against them.

A, FOOLISH QUARREL.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

MAUSHALLTOWN, In., Aug. 8.—A stubbing offray growing out of a small matter occurred Saturday at Illinois. Grove, a few miles from this city, A young fellow, by the name of Roberts and a Dr. Squires got into a controversy over a jackknife, which went so far that Roberts stubbed Squires in the back. The wounded man is not expected to live through the night.

HONORABLY DISCHARGED.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

INDIANAPOLIS, Aug. 8.—William H. Collier, the car-driver who shot and killed the Carney brothers last Monday evening, as detailed in these dispatches, was released this afternoon, the Grand Jury refusing to find an indictment against him. The view of the jury was that Collier acted in self-defense.

A ROBBER KILLED.

Guymas, Aug. 2.—A few American desperados were here some time ago, and left for Alamos, presumably to rob a bullion-train. It has been ascertained since that one of two party, a pentool-looking fellow of about 18, was shot and killed by his partner whilst attempting to put a bullet into his wife's head during a quarrel. Name unknown.

CHARGED WITH HIGHWAY ROBBERY.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Decatur, Ill., Aug. 8.—Owen Roney, a notoriously bad local character, was jailed to-day, charged with highway robbery. His victim was John Brower, and Wqbor's beer-hull yesterday was the scene of the crime.

Regulators Regulated—Negro Highway-man Arrested.
CINCINNATI, August 9.—A special dispatch says fifteen Regulators rode into Grayson, Kentucky, last Saturday, and attempted to assume control. The marshal raised a posse and killed three of the Regulators and captured four.

A colored man giving the name of Ed Anderson has been captured and identified as one of the two who have, in the past few days, been committing so many highway robberies in the vicinity of Oakley and Madisonville, north of this city. His companion escaped. A watch found on him was identified as the one stolen Friday night from Frank Henderson, a son of John Henderson.

A BAD NIGGER,

Whose Neck Should Broken as Soon as He is Caught.

LITTLE ROCK, August 9.—The police have been busy since Saturday working up a case, but so far without success. On Saturday, a negro, a stranger in the city, went to a residence near the corner of Scott and Sixteenth streets and took prisoner a bright mulatto girl. He claimed to be a deputy-sheriff, and served a paper on the girl, who is only about fifteen years of age, and commanded her to go with him to the court. Knowing no better she put on her hat and started. The pretending officer took her into the woods just south of the city, drew a revolver on her, and under penalty of immediate death compelled her to accede to his hellish desires. His purpose accomplished, he left his victim more dead than alive lying in the woods. Some hours after she made her way back to the house, still at the point of death, suffering intense agony. She gave a minute description of the scoundrel, and although seen by several parties no one knows his name or residence.

FORT SMITH, ARK.

An Indian Convicted of Murdering a White Man.

FORT SMITH, August 9.—Sawquaree, a full-blood Sac and Fox Indian, was committed in the United States Court to-day for the murder of an unknown white man in that country in 1879. The jury were out only an hour. It appeared from the evidence that the white man had been employed by Sawquaree to make some rails for him, and while en route to the latter place was attacked by him, shot, and afterward scalped. The scalp was presented about a month later by the noble red man to his nephew, to whom he told the details of the crime. All the witnesses against him were members of his own tribe.

'INDIAN KILLED BY A DEPUTY MARSHAL.

The annexed telegram was received here to-day:

"POWHESKA, L. T., August 9, 1881.

"To V. Dell, United States Marshal:

"I have been in pursuit of Little Buck for five days, and run on him to-day. He, with five others showed fight, resulting in the killing of Little Buck. The Indians are reported in gangs, waiting for me to pull out. I am compelled to wait a day or two for the excitement to subside.

"L. W. MARKS, Deputy Marshal."

Little Buck is one of the chiefs of the Osage tribe of Indians, which, although one of the wealthiest tribes in the Territory, is the most lawless. At the last term of court here six Osages were convicted of horse-stealing, and sentenced to imprisonment at Detroit. Deputy Marshal Marks and his posse, while on their way to this place, were besieged by a band of about 100 Indians, who demanded their release. After much parlying he was allowed to proceed, on a promise that he would not again invade the Territory. It is feared here that he will experience much difficulty in getting out of the country in safety.

Crimes and Casualties.
London, 8.—An express train from Manchester came in collision, to-day, near Blackburn, with the Liverpool and York express. Many people were fearfully injured, several believed to be fatally. There was great destruction of property.

LATER—Five persons were killed, and twenty severely injured, many of whom are not expected to survive.

Paris, 8.—Eleven artillery men were injured, four very severely, by an explosion in the government cartridge factory at Pepignon to-day.

Berlin, 8.—Four houses were burned yesterday and the palace of Count Pourtales was damaged to the extent of half a million marks.

Chicago, 9.—Evening Journal's Jonesville: McLean Manufacturing Company's woolen mill burned this morning. Loss $50,000; insured for $18,000. Fifty hands are out of employment.

Little Rock, 8.—The trial in Perry County has begun. It is a question whether the judge will be brave enough to do justice.

Cincinnati, 8.—Two desperado negroes have been corraled by citizens of Oakley and Madisonville, and their capture is expected.

The Commercial has 30,000 penny subscriptions for Captain Cook.

New York, 8.—The police have ascertained with certainty that Wheelock, the bank check thief, sailed for Bremen on Saturday. Under the treaty between Germany and the United States he cannot be extradited unless his crime can be construed into forgery. It is not known whether he disposed of the letters of credit before leaving the country.

Edward Northrup, a prominent attorney, shot and killed Joseph O'Donnell, clerk of a lumber firm, in the Crawford House, to-day. Northrup had been administrator for the estate of O'Donnell's father. O'Donnell claimed that he was defrauded and a fight ensued. Northrup surrendered.

Havana. 8.—The Spanish mail steamer brought Enrique Paez, recently sentenced to eighteen years' penal servitude at Centa, Morocco, for the fraudulent issue of stamped paper. It has been discovered that he was implicated in the issue of forged paper on the sub-treasury at Matanzas, amounting to $800,000. On Saturday last new frauds in the department of stamped paper were unearthed.

SMITHVILLE, a village eight miles northeast of Wooster, is all torn up over a juvenile shooting scrape. FIFTH EDITION.
LETTER FROM THE MOUNTAINS.
The Pleasure of Summering in the Mountain of the Schuylkill County.
Special Correspondent of the Republican.

TAMAQUA, Pa., July 5th.—Just when or by whom sea side bathing was first introduced, remains a mystery, but we know that to hie away to the mountains was in vogue, away back in the primitive days of the world's history. We read about it in the first books of the Old Testament and it is after all the best way to spend the hot summer months. In the first place it is less costly, and it is less trouble than the sea side watering places. At most of the first class hotels in this region one can obtain substantial board for ten or twelve dollars per week and we do not have to rely on stale vegetables bought in Philadelphia, and carried in the cars away down to the sea shore as they do at Cape May and Atlantic City. Here one may have pure milk and cream, fresh laid eggs, good wholesome butter, and all kinds of vegetables fresh from the gardens. We are enjoying splendid weather just now, just warm enough during the day and the night cool enough to sleep well, while such things as mosquitos are unknown. No one could wish for a better appetite than a bracing walk over the mountain side will give hem if taken in the early morning. The scenery is delightful and it is grand to see old "Sol" rising out of his misty bed beautifully tinting every little cloud and tree.

It is surprising how each succeeding event helps us to forget those that have preceded it. This is brought very forcibly to ones mind, in looking back four or five years, then the "Mollie Maguires," had full sway. No one felt safe and although your correspondent did not live hereabouts then, their whole history is reinvested with interest by hearing the people talk about them, and to read the book that Allan Pinkerton wrote, from notes taken by his detective Jas. McParlan who spent several years with the "Mollies" and became one of their most trusted friends, makes one think truly, "truth is stranger than fiction." Your correspondent visited several places where murders took place. He stood on the spot where in 1876 John P. Jones was murdered by Kerrigan, Doyle and Kelly, as he was going to his daily work. He saw the lamp post where B. F. Yost was climbing up to put out the light when in a minute he was shot dead by McGeehan, a "Mollie." He saw the rum holes where the "Mollies" used to meet which by the way are still run by the widows of some that were hung, and where McParlan, alias Jas. McKenna, used to lay around drunk to all appearances, but awake and sober, as they afterwards found out. But the days of the "Mollies" are over, they will never organize again, because they won't trust one another. McParlan was a dose they will never forget.

The P. & R. R. R. Co. are putting a very handsome fence around the open lot adjoining the depot. The 4th passed without any accidents. There was a mock circus parade, which for originality and fun making "took the rag off the bush" of anything your correspondent ever saw.

The attempted assassination of the President created intense feeling here. In Mahaney city, near here, a man named Refowitch came near near being lynched for making some disloyal remark. They had the rope around his neck when he begged so hard that they let him off.

Co. B. 8th Regt. P. V. had their yearly inspection of arms last week, and in the evening gave a grand supper and bail at the U. S. Hotel.

A shopkeeper in Mahanoy City, who was reported to have made some remarks approving of the assassination of President Garfield, was waited on by a large deputation of excited citizens on Saturday with the intention of administering summary punishment. When the crowd appeared, he denied having used any expression of the kind, and through the persuasion of a number of the citizens, he was not molested.

Norwich, N. J., July 4.—Michael Hill, aged 70 years, was jailed in this city a few weeks ago for larceny. During Sheriff Hazard's absence on Thursday Hill escaped from his cell and went to his home in Sherburne, N. J., to provide for his family, who are in a destitute condition. The Sheriff returned, and, learning that the prisoner had fled, he started in pursuit. Three miles from Sherburne he met Hill on his return trip to the jail. Having provided the necessaries of life for a family of seven persons, he was satisfied to return and serve out his sentence. He is now in jail.

Lawlessness at Girard.

Mr. Editor: On Saturday, the 16th instant, three or four evildisposed persons living in and near Girard, committed a very grave offence against the peace of our community, as well as indignity to the law, by using personal violence against a colored man from an adjoining parish. Pretending to arrest him by authority of law, and decoying him out of town to the river bank, they lacerated his beck with savage cruelty, leaving gasher deep and long, the scars of which will be as enduring as life. It behooves all good citizens to set their faces against such acts and to use due diligence to bring the offenders to justice.

A CITIZEN.

The above communication needs to comment. It is written by as good man as there is in the parish, who would not misrepresent facts, and calls loudly upon the officers of law to vindicate both the law and the good name of our parish.

Fish Fries.

Our people seem to have become very fond of fish of late, or of piscatorial sport. Last Wednesday we followed a small party up on Boeuf river to a place back of Mrs. Edwards' plantation, arriving there just before they began collecting the fish together for the "fry." The catch was small, but the ladies fried them very nicely, we had good coffee, and, with other things to help out, we managed to make a good meal, which we enjoy as much as any we ever ate. We all relished our dinner; all were cheerful and disposed to participate in a little good natured humor at each other's expense, and all came home well pleased with our day's sport and recreation.

Thursday we joined some of the same party, with an addition of a few others, and went up on Dead Lake, near Lafourche Ferry, where we caught an abundance of fish—more than we could all eat, though we did our best to get away with our full share. It was a very pleasant affair—as pleasant as that of the previous day; but on our return home our horse got very sick, and we thought for a while we would have to walk home and lose a horse too, but we managed to get home, after some delay.

On Friday morning, as we write this, another party are on their way to Cypress bayou to have a fish fry—hope they too will have a good time.

SUMMARY OF STATE NEWS.
Gleanings from the Louisiana Press.

Morgan City Review: The great pile driver of the railroad bridge is now driving the third tier of piles.

Iberville South: A few nights since the premises of Rev. Father Harnais of this place were broken into and two fine horses carried off. Pursuit was made next morning but no tidings could be heard of the rogues.

DeSoto Democrat: On Saturday last near this place on the railroad, a man by the name of Dobson shot two men; Sol Neblus was shot in the hip and Charles Gaskins in the hand. Both of the wounded men are doing well. Dobson made his escape.

Marksville Bulletin: Mules, horses and stock are dying in this community from an unknown disease, supposed by some to be charbon... The crop of corn will be a poor one this year. Many planters consider if they make a half crop they will be doing well.

St. Landry Argus: Monday evening the two Avery boys, who were convicted of perjury and sentenced to eight years in the State penitentiary two or three years since, broke from the line while at work on the railroad just across the Courtableau, when one of the gaurds fired, inflicted three flesh wounds in the arm, shoulder and neck of one of them who was recaptured; but the other succeeded in making his escape.

Assumption Pioneer: Two colored prisoners, Pleasant Croom and John Henry, confined in jail here, escaped last night.... Dr. Francis E. Malthiot, a native of this parish, died at Covington, La., on the 20th instant. His distinguished
night. Dr. Francis E. Maimor, a native of this parish, died at Covington, La., on the 20th instant. His distinguished uncle, Wm. Reed Mills of New Orleans, accompanied the body from Covington to the Episcopal cemetery here, where, in the presence of many friends and kindred, it was consigned to the tomb.

Assumption Pioneer: The Court of Appeals was in session here on the 5th instant. There being no cases on the docket, the term lasted just fifteen minutes. Judges Blake and Dumartrait looked genial, rosy and vigorous as ever. Immediately after the close of their exhausting judicial labors here they embarked for Thibodaux in a primitive vehicle, called a horse and buggy in the Attakapas regions, but by more advanced civilizations a gohickle and creole tacky.

A deck-hand on the steamer St. Mary, while assisting in landing a barrel of whisky at this point, unfortunately slipped, causing the whole weight of the barrel to fall upon his arm, which was fearfully crushed and broken.

Shreveport Telegram: A Negro named Spence, aged about 18 years, was found hung in the neighborhood of Frog Level a few days ago. He had twice attempted to enter the room of an orphan girl residing with Mr. J. B. Spearman, and had once been tied and got away. A few nights ago he made another attempt to enter the room, which was at the time occupied by two lady friends of the family, who had come on a visit, the orphan girl having been removed to another room. This last attempt resulted in his capture and he was dealt with as he should have been....A colored man named Robert Smith was drowned at the ferry landing. He lost his balance while standing on the edge of the wharf and fell into the river....Squire Coleman, a colored man living about a mile from town, on the Bauman place, was shot and killed by Charley Johnson, paramour of Coleman's wife. The murderer is still at large.

LOUISIANA.
The assessment rolls of West Feliciana show a total property of $1,148,-672.

The St. Mary Review declares that hundreds of green alligator hides are shipped from that point weekly.

The whooping cough still prevails in East Feliciana, and has been the cause of the death of a number of children.

Some dissatisfaction exists in Grant parish at the fact that several teachers hold positions on the Parish School Board.

A negro man and a mule were struck by lightning on the plantation of Mrs. Moreland, in Tensas arish, last Saturday.

A negro named Spence wasynched in the neighborhood of Frog Levee, Caddo parish, last week for an attempt at rape.

Monroe has just numbered its houses. It proposes to supplement this by placing the names of the streets on the corners.

Robert Smith, while crossing the Red river near the Pough place, in Caddo parish, fell into the water and was drowned last week.

The name of the station on the New Orleans and Pacific has been changed from Hobgood City to Grand Cave City. The town has been laid out and lots are now offered for sale.

The police jury of Caddo levied a tax last week of 7% mills; they also passed an ordinance levying a special tax of 3% mills for the payment of the amount due on parish bonds and judgments against the parish.

Last Saturday on the road about two miles from Minden, Webb Gamble shot and killed Frank Elkins. The shot took effect in the abdomen, and the wounded man died next day. The shooting was done about dusk. Elkins and Gamble were brothers-in-law.

The election in the parish of St. Martin for the removal of the parish seat from St. Martinsville to Breaux Bridge, held on the sixteenth instant, resulted in a grand victory for St. Martinsville, where the court-house has been located for nearly a half century.

A most atrocious crime was committed Saturday night at Kingstown, a small hamlet in DeSoto parish, about twelve miles northeast of Mansfield. M. Judd Scott, a young merchant doing business in Kingstown left his boarding house about 9 o'clock p. m., going to his store, where it was his custom to sleep. On Sunday morning his body was discovered lying about half way between Mrs 'Beard's, where he boarded, and his store. The top of his head had been almost entirely blown off by a gun shot. The brains were scattered around, and hogs had partly devoured his body. His store and safe keys had been taken and it was subsequently ascertained that the store and safe had been opened. No goods have been missed, and it is not known how much has been taken.
